subject: QBR ops: slot hedges, burst scenarios & GPU unit-econ asks
messages:
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
To: Lauren Bishop <lauren_bishop@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 10 Jun 2029 08:12:00 +0000
Subject: QBR ops: slot hedges, burst scenarios & GPU unit-econ asks

Team — prepping the infra section for next week’s QBR. Attached is a working workbook (2029_QBR_capacity_hedges_v2.xlsx) with scenario tabs. I want leadership alignment on the operational hedges we present (reserved vs burst, slot sizing, and fallback model policies). High-level asks: 

1) Confirm runway target: do we present a conservative runway (30% buffer on forecast) or an aggressive runway (10% buffer + market-dependent burst)? I’ve modeled both.
2) Approve up to 120 reserved A100-equivalent GPUs for Dedicated pools (monthly commit) vs keeping burst capacity at current levels (burst = up to +50% of steady). See "Reserve_v_Burst" tab.
3) Approve a Tiered fallback policy for high-load SLO protection: fallback to quantized M-family for non-critical routes; automatic canary to smaller model family at 90th percentile queue depth.

Unit-econ summary (more detail in the workbook):
- Baseline (no quant, default batching): $9.80 per 1M tokens served (hosted average)
- Add continuous batching (target batch=32): estimated per-1M cost drops 28% (to ~$7.06) based on the bench runs — but note 95th-latency increases ~12–18ms for interactive routes.
- KV prefix cache impact: modeled hit rates at 30/50/70% -> cost reductions of ~9% / ~18% / ~26% respectively. Current prod measured hit ~42% for the chat use-case.
- Reserved capacity vs on-demand spot: reserved reduces GPU unit cost by ~24% in my model but requires commit windows and increases burn risk during traffic downturns.

Open risks I call out in the workbook: a 3x traffic spike (week-long) pushes utilization to >160% of committed capacity in the conservative reserve plan; burst buffers mitigate this but at higher unit cost. Also, continuous batching gives the biggest long-run savings only if tail-latency stays within SLOs — we need routing rules to keep interactive paths on lower batch targets.

Please review the workbook and the "Decision_asks" sheet. Can you each reply with: 1) your preferred runway (conservative/aggressive), 2) whether you approve the 120 GPU reserve ask, and 3) any redlines on fallback policy? I’d like decisions by EOD Tuesday so we have time to update slides.

Thanks,
Karthik

> Team — prepping the infra section for next week’s QBR. Attached is a working workbook...

Thanks for the tidy model, Karthik — a few quick notes from the leadership side:

- Runway preference: conservative runway (30% buffer). We present that as the primary plan and show an aggressive hedge as an appendix. Leadership wants to see the worst-case contingency clearly.
- 120 reserved GPUs: I'm inclined to approve a partial commit instead of the full ask. Propose staging: commit 60 now, hold the other 60 conditional on the 60-day traffic trend. Please add a stage gating row in the workbook with clear metrics (utilization band, revenue signal).
- Fallback policy: fine with quantized fallback for background/async routes. For interactive product routes, we should have an automated A/B rollback if p95 latency degrades by >20% post-fallback.

Action: can you add a small heatmap (traffic x reserve level -> runway gap) and one-slide note about how caching TTL changes affect the 30/60/90-day savings? Link the heatmap in the slide deck so we can surface it on a single QBR slide.

-Lauren

Karthik / Lauren — quick finance/control notes: 

- Reserve economics look reasonable; agree with staggered commit (60 now, 60 conditional). From a treasury perspective, we need sensitivity for a 30–60% revenue dip scenario (how fast can we unwind or repurpose reserved capacity; cost hit if we pay the commit but idle at 40% utilization).
- Please model a 72-hour 3x spike and show contingency steps (activate burst, shift non-critical routes to quantized models, and rate-limit low-priority clients). We should also include a rotational canary schedule so fallbacks are exercised weekly and we avoid surprises at scale.

One operational ask: include an explicit plan for autoscaling cooldowns and queue-depth thresholds that trigger fallback. If the QBR slide can show the trigger thresholds, risk tolerance will be easier to communicate.

-Vivek

Head of Infrastructure Ops

Subject: Re: QBR ops: slot hedges, burst scenarios & GPU unit-econ asks

Folks — ran the requested microbench and a 48-hour slot soak last week; quick summary (more detail in the Grafana dash linked in related_links):

- Prod steady-state utilization: 78% (avg), with spotty p95 spikes around predictable batch windows.
- Continuous batching (config: batch target 32, max wait 40ms) increased aggregated throughput 2.1x vs batch=1 on our L-family models. Tradeoff: p95 for interactive routes moved from 190ms -> 205–220ms depending on cold-KV behavior.
- KV cache: current hit ~42% for the chat pipeline. When we increased TTL and prefetch heuristics during the soak, hit improved to 58% and end-to-end token compute dropped ~16% for repeat prompts.
- Stress scenario (simulated 3x traffic for 72 hours): with current reserve=0 and burst cap only, tail latencies breached SLO for high-priority routes within 7 hours. With reserve=60 GPUs and the fallback policy engaged (quantized M-family for low-priority routes + KV TTL tuning), we kept p95 within SLO but unit cost rose ~36% for the period.

I can run another 72-hour soak next week using the staged reserve plan (60 commit) and the cooldown thresholds Vivek suggested. If we want, I’ll add a short appendix slide with the batch-size sensitivity chart and the cache-hit vs cost curve.

-Marissa
